title: Job Demands His Day in Court
overview: Job rejects his friends' claim that his suffering proves he sinned, and boldly asks God himself for a fair hearing.

parts.label: Worthless doctors (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: Job says he knows as much as his friends do and needs no lecture from them. They came like doctors to heal him, but their false explanations only hurt, so silence would be their wisest move.

parts.label: Lying to defend God (vv. 6-12)
parts.note: The friends think they are defending God by insisting Job's suffering proves he sinned, but Job says lying on God's behalf is still lying, and God would call them to account for it. Their well known sayings are as flimsy as ashes, and their arguments crumble like walls of clay.

parts.label: Speaking whatever the cost (vv. 13-19)
parts.note: Job decides to speak his mind even if it costs him his life, and he trusts that a fraud would never dare stand before God the way he wants to. Verse 15 can be read from the Hebrew as either "I will hope in him" or "I have no hope," but either way Job insists on defending himself to God's face.

parts.label: Two requests to God (vv. 20-22)
parts.note: Job turns to God and asks two things: take away the hand that is crushing him, and stop terrifying him. Then he will stop hiding and face God in court, either answering God's charges or speaking first and hearing God's reply.

parts.label: Show me my crime (vv. 23-27)
parts.note: Job asks God to name his sins and explain why he is treated as an enemy, picturing himself as a fallen leaf still chased by the wind. He feels like a prisoner, with a bitter sentence written against him, punished even for the sins of his youth, his feet locked in wooden stocks and his every step watched.

parts.label: Wearing away (v. 28)
parts.note: Job widens his view from himself to all people, who waste away like something rotten or like cloth eaten by moths. This line leads into the next chapter's reflection on how short and fragile human life is.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Job's bold challenge to God here is a model of honest faith or a sign that his suffering pushed him to overstep, which some see God correcting later in the book.
think: When someone is suffering, what makes an explanation feel helpful rather than hurtful?
